body:
Scout disposition: keep two estimands explicit. (A) a task-conditioned perceptual boundary track calibrated to a declared human instruction and grain; (B) an evidence-backed resolved narrative hierarchy that may use broader constraints. The resolved hierarchy must never be recycled as human-consensus gold, and a rater vote fraction is not automatically a calibrated probability.

Current ownership already looks right: features owns aligned signals and missingness, acquire owns provider/task proposals and receipts, and story owns accepted hierarchy. I would not add a segment module until a second real consumer forces a stable optimizer abstraction. The present level: Int surface is too weak for the external scientific estimand: small-event versus large-event instructions are task semantics, not merely anonymous hierarchy depths. That requirement needs an ADR/public-vocabulary decision before implementation. Topic-model output should likewise remain a feature-side view until a corpus-query consumer establishes a core identity need.

Validation should retain per-rater series and use leave-story or leave-story-family-out evaluation, with provider-family holdout for machine proposals. Report tolerance curves rather than one F1, plus Pk/WindowDiff, count bias, Brier/calibration, hierarchy-constraint violations, and a split-half human ceiling. Repeated LLM calls are provider/config-clustered votes, not independent human raters; effective sample size must not equal raw run count.

Adversarial gates I would require: kill a cue-only predictor; kill right-count/wrong-gap placements; distinguish absent signal from observed zero; preserve retry/dedup receipts; reject a flat solution when nested structure is required; reject uncalibrated vote fractions presented as probabilities; and expose story/fame leakage plus provider drift. StoryAtlas should show the raw perceptual track separately from selected hierarchy brackets, with alternatives/rejections, coverage, missingness, and receipts visible rather than visually morphing one artifact into the other.
